analysis.one_liner: Lets auto insurers sell cheaper no-fault policies that waive drivers' right to sue for pain and suffering.
analysis.headline: The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship and a Senate committee hearing in September 1996, but never got a committee vote or floor action, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overridden state law to let auto insurers sell a new 'personal protection' policy: drivers who picked it would be paid their out-of-pocket losses by their own insurer regardless of fault, but would give up the right to sue the other driver for pain and suffering. Supporters, led by Senator McConnell, promised it would cut insurance premiums — the bill even let a state opt out entirely if its insurance regulator found premiums would not drop by at least 30%. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held one hearing but never voted on it, and it expired with the 104th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Auto insurers gain a federally authorized product that converts open-ended injury lawsuits into fixed first-party claims capped at out-of-pocket economic losses. Drivers, especially in high-premium urban areas, would have gained if the promised premium reductions materialized — the bill's own opt-out mechanism assumed a 30% cut. Trial lawyers and anyone injured in a crash who would have wanted to recover for pain and suffering lose the most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Auto insurers; drivers seeking lower premiums

how_it_helps.text: Drivers choosing the new 'personal protection' coverage would be paid their own policy's net economic losses — medical bills, lost earnings, replacement services — without having to prove fault, with late claims accruing 50% annual interest from the insurer [S3].

The bill projected large premium savings, and let a state escape the law entirely if its insurance regulator found, after a public hearing within 60 days, that statewide average personal-injury premiums would not fall by at least 30% [S3].

The bill's findings argued the tort system imposes a 'tort tax' that falls hardest on low-income and urban drivers, driving some to drive uninsured, and that a choice-based system would cut those costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured in crashes under the new coverage lose the right to recover noneconomic damages — pain, suffering, emotional distress, loss of companionship — against the other driver, keeping only verifiable out-of-pocket losses. Plaintiffs' trial lawyers lose the contingency-fee cases that pain-and-suffering claims generate, and health insurers and workers' compensation programs would absorb costs that auto insurers no longer pay, since 'net economic loss' excludes amounts already paid by those sources.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured crash victims and trial lawyers

drawbacks.text: Choosing the new coverage means waiving tort claims for noneconomic losses, so an injured person could no longer recover for pain and suffering, emotional distress, or loss of companionship from a negligent driver — only verifiable out-of-pocket losses [S3].

'Net economic loss' excludes anything paid by health insurance, workers' compensation, or disability programs, so victims whose medical bills were already covered by their health plan could recover less from the at-fault driver's side, shifting costs onto those programs [S3].

A motorist's choice binds resident relatives, with consent merely implied when an adult relative rides in the household's vehicle, and insurers are authorized to push uniformity across a household — so one policyholder's waiver can limit others' legal rights [S3].

The bill preempts contrary state law nationwide, overriding states' own no-fault and tort arrangements unless a state affirmatively opts out within a 60-day window after enactment — a narrow window that made an opt-out difficult in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real: the tort auto-insurance system does produce high legal costs, slow payouts, and premiums that hit urban and low-income drivers hardest, and a credible estimate of 30% premium savings is baked into the bill's own opt-out test. The cost is equally real — injured people would give up recovery for pain and suffering, the most unpredictable but often the largest part of a serious injury claim, and costs would shift to health insurers and government programs whose payments are excluded from 'net economic loss.' Whether the trade favors the public depends on how much premiums actually fell, which the bill leaves to insurers and state regulators to demonstrate after the fact.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee, which held a hearing in September 1996 but never voted on it, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator McConnell introduced the bill on June 11, 1996, joined by three cosponsors — Senator Dole (R) and Senators Moynihan and Lieberman (D) — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1] [S5].
The Commerce Committee held hearings on September 24, 1996, printed as S.Hrg. 104-613, but took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor consideration [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trial lawyers and the existing tort system's legal remedies for injured drivers survived untouched; auto insurers did not get the federally authorized waiver product, and drivers did not get the promised premium cuts either. State insurance regulators kept full authority over auto insurance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trial lawyers; victims' lawsuit rights preserved

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Auto Choice Reform Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Bob Dole
for.role: Cosponsor; Senate Majority Leader until June 1996 and 1996 Republican presidential nominee

for.name: Sens. Daniel Patrick Moynihan and Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from two prominent Senate Democrats.

for.name: Auto insurance industry
for.role: Principal beneficiary of auto-choice tort reform
for.what_they_did: Backed federal auto-choice legislation that would cap injury payouts at economic losses; auto choice was a long-standing industry legislative priority in the 1990s.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee (Chair Larry Pressler, R-SD)
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on September 24, 1996, but never scheduled a markup or committee vote, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Trial lawyers (plaintiffs' bar)
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal auto-choice proposals that would waive injured drivers' right to sue for pain and suffering, the core of contingency-fee auto injury practice.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — McConnell and Dole (R) joined by Moynihan and Lieberman (D) — and the bill died quietly in committee without any recorded vote to measure partisan division.

industries.note: The bill would have let insurers sell federally protected policies that convert injury claims into fixed first-party payments capped at out-of-pocket losses, eliminating open-ended pain-and-suffering liability. Its gain comes directly from paying injured people less, even as supporters promised drivers 30% lower premiums.

The new coverage waives tort claims for noneconomic damages, eliminating the pain-and-suffering cases that make up much of the plaintiffs' bar's auto-accident work. Their interest in the bill ran alongside crash victims' right to full legal recovery.

industries.industry: Health insurers and workers' compensation programs
industries.note: Because 'net economic loss' excludes amounts already paid by health plans, disability programs, and workers' compensation, auto insurers would pay less while those programs absorb costs they might otherwise recover. Injured people with existing coverage would recover less in total.
